obstacles: Widespread and important natural system have no numerical cutoff in the text.
A model that looks like a natural pattern does not identify the natural system's actual rule.
assessments.rationale: Published proofs show universality in several simple abstract systems, so the abstract half can be sampled now. The natural half asks for universality of real systems, and existing work mostly offers models rather than demonstrated mechanisms. The quantifiers are too open, and the proved examples too selective, for the full statement to be confirmed or refuted.

assessments.operationalization: Implement the published 19-color, range-2 rule and the block encoding that stores a target rule and cell state. Compare the decoded evolution with the target cellular automaton. Agreement for arbitrary colors and neighborhoods, via the stated reduction to a binary larger-neighborhood rule, confirms the claim; a mismatch refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: public source of the 19-color rule table and the block encoding

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: open simulator in which the universal rule and the target rules can be run and compared

obstacles: The full rule table is large, and some neighborhood combinations are excluded by the initial-condition invariant, so a checker must follow that invariant.
assessments.rationale: The claim is an existence claim with an explicit construction: a fixed rule, a block encoding, and a uniform way to add colors and neighbors. Both pieces are published and can be executed. Checking elementary targets and the color-reduction step is a finite programming task, and a single failed emulation of a covered target would refute the claim.

assessments.operationalization: For each named family, implement the published cellular-automaton encoding and test agreement of decoded steps with the target system on a suite of programs. Confirm if mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution and tag systems, register machines, logic circuits, and memory behave as specified; refute if any named family has a program the construction cannot follow.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published diagrams and rules for each emulation construction

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for running the cellular-automaton side of each construction

obstacles: A complete stored-program computer is only sketched as a composition of the register, logic, and memory pieces, so that last step needs an explicit architecture to check.
assessments.rationale: Each named family is given as a finite encoding whose traces can be compared with the system it is supposed to copy. That comparison uses public rules and ordinary simulation. The further statement that a practical computer can be assembled from those pieces is standard once the pieces check out, though the book leaves the composite machine schematic.

assessments.operationalization: Compare growth rates. A substitution step may multiply the number of elements by a constant greater than one, while one step of a cellular automaton of radius r adds at most a fixed number of cells. Lockstep emulation is refuted by this inequality for expanding systems, and would be confirmed only by a construction that updates every substitution step in one cellular-automaton step for every such system.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for measuring pattern width per step against substitution length

obstacles: The bound forbids one-step-per-step emulation of expanding systems; it says nothing against emulations that use increasingly many cellular-automaton steps.
assessments.rationale: The argument is a counting proof and applies to every cellular automaton, because every fixed radius grows by a bounded amount per step. It can be written in a page and illustrated by running any expanding substitution system beside any cellular automaton. The claim is exactly this general impossibility, which the inequality settles.

assessments.operationalization: Treat a neighbor-independent substitution system as iteration of a fixed morphism and show that its evolution diagram is self-similar by construction, hence repetitive or nested, and therefore not the evolution of rule 30. Separately, implement the neighbor-dependent construction and check that it reproduces rule 90 and rule 30. A non-nested neighbor-independent diagram would refute the first half; a failed copy would refute the second.

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of morphic and automatic sequences generated by neighbor-independent substitution

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published neighbor-dependent substitution rules that copy rules 90 and 30

obstacles: Nested has to be read as the self-similar geometry of morphism iteration; a claim about every scalar sequence derived from such a system would be broader than the evolution diagram.
assessments.rationale: The evolution diagram of a neighbor-independent substitution system is produced by uniform replacement, so its nested or ultimately repetitive form is a structural theorem, and rule 30's diagram is not of that form. The neighbor-dependent direction is an explicit, small construction that can be checked step by step. Both directions are within a short proof or a short program.

assessments.operationalization: Verify two lemmas: a universal cellular automaton exists, and each listed family has a construction that emulates an arbitrary cellular automaton. The emulator of the universal cellular automaton is then universal. The implication fails only if some listed family cannot emulate every cellular automaton or if no universal cellular automaton exists.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published emulation constructions for mobile automata, Turing machines, substitution systems, tag systems, symbolic systems, and register machines

candidate_datasets.name: Complex Systems
candidate_datasets.role: archive containing the checked universality proof for rule 110, which supplies one universal cellular automaton

obstacles: The cyclic-tag route is staged through tag systems and Turing machines, so a check must follow the whole chain rather than one picture.
assessments.rationale: The abstract implication is immediate once both lemmas are granted, and each lemma is a published construction rather than an existence guess. Rule 110 supplies a fully argued universal cellular automaton, and the book gives the emulators for the listed families. Reviewing those constructions is specialist work measured in weeks, not an open research problem.

assessments.operationalization: Encode a register-machine state as an integer of the published form and apply the remainder-selected arithmetic map. Confirm if successive integers track the program counter and both registers for a universal register machine; refute if the map diverges from that trace. Universality then follows from the known universality of register machines.

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld FRACTRAN
candidate_datasets.role: public account of a remainder-and-arithmetic system already shown to be universal

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: explicit modulus-30 rule and the integer encoding of a register machine

obstacles: The encoding uses a particular modulus and prime powers, so a checker has to test that program, not an arbitrary Collatz-like map.
assessments.rationale: The system is a concrete integer map with a stated correspondence to register-machine steps, the same idea as FRACTRAN. Traces can be compared for as many steps as one wants, and the reduction to a universal register machine is finite. That is a constructive proof, checkable by a short program.

assessments.operationalization: For the named families, check mutual emulation of a universal member. Confirm if each family can realize exactly the Turing-computable input-output maps; refute if some named family computes a non-Turing function or cannot emulate a Turing machine.

candidate_datasets.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Church-Turing thesis
candidate_datasets.role: statement of the equivalence of the standard universal models

candidate_datasets.name: UniversalityDB
candidate_datasets.role: formalized simulation edges among Turing machines, tag systems, and cellular automata

obstacles: Equivalence of computable functions does not settle equivalence of runtime, or of behavior from typical initial conditions.
assessments.rationale: For the families actually constructed in the chapter, mutual emulation is a chain of explicit reductions, and the Church-Turing equivalence says they determine the same class of computations. The constructions are public and finite. The word essentially leaves the boundary of the class slightly soft, but not soft enough to block a check of the systems named.

assessments.operationalization: Restrict capability to the set of input-output maps realizable with some encoding. Confirm if every Turing-universal system realizes exactly the partial recursive functions, so a more elaborate universal rule adds none; refute if some standard universal system computes a non-recursive function or if two universal systems realize different sets of maps.

candidate_datasets.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Church-Turing thesis
candidate_datasets.role: reference for the theorem that standard universal models compute the same functions

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld, Universal Turing Machine
candidate_datasets.role: definition of universality used to compare repertoires of systems

obstacles: Cost in time and space still depends on the rule, so a reading in terms of efficiency is not settled by extensional equivalence.
Intermediate Turing degrees show that not every non-simple system sits at this threshold; the claim concerns systems that have already passed it.
assessments.rationale: Within ordinary discrete models, universality means the ability to emulate a Turing machine, and any two such systems emulate each other. That theorem is textbook material and directly matches the claim that the set of computations stops growing once the threshold is passed. It does not say that more complicated rules are useless for speed or for ease of encoding.

assessments.operationalization: Check a published reduction from an arbitrary cyclic tag system, or an arbitrary Turing machine, to initial conditions of rule 110, and check that glider collisions implement the tag steps. Successful emulation confirms universality; a gap that leaves some tag systems unemulated would refute the proof as a proof of the full claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: published proof that rule 110 emulates cyclic tag systems and hence Turing machines

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for replaying the glider collisions used in the construction

obstacles: The construction constrains tag blocks and then removes the constraint by a further reduction, so a partial replay of one picture is not the whole proof.
assessments.rationale: Universality of this one rule is a mathematical statement with a published, cited proof and an explicit glider construction. A competent team can audit that proof and resimulate its components with existing software. The result covers the rule as stated, including emulation of arbitrary cyclic tag systems after the bookkeeping reduction.

assessments.operationalization: Choose explicit simplicity bounds, such as elementary cellular automata or Turing machines with a bounded state-symbol product, and compute the fraction with a finished universality proof or a finished non-universality proof. The prediction is supported if that fraction is high inside several families, and weakened if proofs keep universality rare among simple rules.

candidate_datasets.name: UniversalityDB
candidate_datasets.role: census of simple systems whose universality has been formally recorded

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: proof for one elementary rule and the small Turing machines reduced to it

obstacles: Common, wide range, and rather simple are not given numerical boundaries.
Failure to prove universality is not evidence of non-universality.
assessments.rationale: Rule 110 and a handful of other simple systems are known to be universal, so the prediction can be probed inside small families. Most simple rules are still unclassified, and there is no measure under which an overwhelming share of simple rules has been shown universal. Existing proofs therefore test a sample, not the claim that universality is common across simple programs.

assessments.operationalization: Order rules by a fixed complexity of the rule table and score each evolution by a fixed measure such as compressibility or persistence of interacting localized structures. The claim is supported if the measure plateaus once a low rule complexity is passed, and refuted if it keeps rising across that range.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: enumerator and simulator for elementary and totalistic rules ordered by rule complexity

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: published sequences from simple rules, for comparing compressibility as rule complexity increases

obstacles: Behavioral complexity has several standard measures, and they need not plateau together.
Enumeration is feasible only for small rule spaces; larger neighborhoods are a different sample.
assessments.rationale: Small rule spaces can be enumerated and scored with public software in weeks, which is enough to test the predicted plateau for elementary cellular automata and small Turing machines. As complex as it will ever be depends on the chosen score, and a plateau in one family does not cover every kind of simple program. The result is a family of proxy tests rather than a decision of the full prediction.

assessments.operationalization: Define class 4 by persistent, interacting, localized structures on a quiescent or periodic background. Confirm the claim only if every such rule has a universality proof, and refute it by one class-4 rule proved incapable of emulating a Turing machine.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: completed universality proof for the class-4 rule 110

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: pattern collection and simulator for other class-4 rules, including the Game of Life

obstacles: Class 4 is diagnosed from pictures, so borderline rules can be labeled either way.
Not finding a glider computer does not prove that a class-4 rule is not universal.
assessments.rationale: Universality is settled for rule 110 and for some two-dimensional class-4 rules such as the Game of Life, so particular cases are checkable. The claim is about every class-4 rule, and each new proof is a research project rather than a standard analysis. A single rigorously non-universal class-4 rule would refute it, but no such classification exists for the class as a whole.

assessments.operationalization: Simulate all 256 elementary rules from random and simple seeds and flag persistent localized structures that interact. Confirm if only rule 110 and its three color or reflection equivalents meet a pre-registered class-4 test, and confirm the second clause by sampling totalistic rules with more colors or a larger neighborhood and finding many such examples.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: exhaustive simulation of the 256 elementary rules and sampling of totalistic rules

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: published survey figures and the identification of rules 110, 124, 137, and 193

obstacles: Rule 54 and long transients sit on the boundary of clear class-4 behavior, so the word clear has to be fixed before the count is unique.
A finite run can miss a localized structure that appears only from a rare seed.
assessments.rationale: The elementary half is a finite census of 256 rules, and the four-rule symmetry class is an exact mathematical object. Sampling a step up in colors or neighborhood, including totalistic rules, is the same kind of computation and directly tests the claim that class-4 behavior then becomes easy to find. The remaining uncertainty is the verbal boundary around clear, not missing data.

assessments.operationalization: Formalize class 1 and class 2 as evolution that, for every initial condition, becomes uniform or periodic with a bound depending only on the rule. Prove that such a system has a finite effective memory and cannot emulate a Turing machine. A universality construction inside that class would refute the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: enumeration of elementary class-1 and class-2 rules whose periods and light cones can be checked

candidate_datasets.name: MathWorld, Universal Turing Machine
candidate_datasets.role: reference requirement that a universal system emulate arbitrary Turing-machine computations

obstacles: Some rules usually called class 2 carry signals arbitrarily far, so non-universality then rests on the form of the reachable configurations rather than on a strict distance bound.
assessments.rationale: If the class is defined by ultimately uniform or repetitive behavior for every input, non-universality is a theorem: only finitely much information about the input survives, or the surviving information is periodic. That argument can be checked on the elementary examples by computing periods and dependence cones. The book's phrase about limited distance is slightly too narrow for shifting class-2 rules, but those rules still fail universality for the same periodicity reason.

assessments.operationalization: For additive rules such as 90 and 150, use the linear representation over the field with two elements and check that the configuration at 2^k steps is a fixed superposition of shifts of the initial condition. Confirm non-universality because some computable spacetime diagrams never return to that form; refute it by exhibiting a universal computation inside an additive rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Martin, Odlyzko, and Wolfram 1984
candidate_datasets.role: algebraic analysis of additive cellular automata, including the superposition structure used in the argument

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: numerical check that rules 90 and 150 at powers of two reproduce shifts of the initial row

obstacles: The algebraic proof covers linear rules directly; purely nested but nonlinear rules need a separate definition of nested before the same conclusion applies.
assessments.rationale: For rules 90 and 150 the state at dyadic times is an explicit linear function of the initial condition, a fact proved in the additive-cellular-automaton literature and easy to recompute. Behaviors that do not collapse in that way cannot occur, so those rules are not universal. The wider nested class is settled in the same way once nested is identified with a substitution or linear schema, which is the argument the book gives.

assessments.operationalization: Enumerate rule 54's initial conditions in the book's order through the hundred millionth, run each to a pre-set horizon, and classify the evolution as periodic, nested with an explicit formula, or neither. Finding one evolution that is neither refutes the report; agreement through the whole range confirms it.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: engine for replaying rule 54 from the enumerated initial conditions

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: numbering examples and closed forms, such as initial condition 291, that define the patterns being checked

obstacles: A finite time cutoff can mistake a long transient for nesting, or miss structure that appears later.
Fundamentally more complicated has to be replaced by a mechanical classifier before two reruns must agree.
assessments.rationale: The claim is a finite census, not an assertion that rule 54 is simple for every seed. Regenerating a hundred million short evolutions is ordinary computation, and the book already supplies formulas for the patterns it highlights. The judgment more complicated must be frozen into a classifier, but once that is done the census can confirm or refute the stated bound.

assessments.operationalization: Call a system fundamentally repetitive or nested only if every evolution has a proved periodic or substitution form, and call it universal if it emulates a Turing machine. The expectation is refuted by one system outside that class that is proved non-universal, and it is not confirmed by complexity of appearance alone.

candidate_datasets.name: UniversalityDB
candidate_datasets.role: record of which non-nested systems have an actual universality proof

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: completed case, rule 110, against which harder cases can be compared

obstacles: More or less any and in the end make the quantifier and the deadline undefined.
Absence of a universality proof does not prove non-universality, so failed searches do not refute the expectation.
assessments.rationale: Particular systems can be placed on one side or the other when a proof exists, as with rule 110 and the additive rules. The claim covers essentially every non-nested system, and for a typical system neither universality nor a hidden nested form is known. Existing proofs therefore speak to examples, while the general expectation stays out of reach of a finite computation.

assessments.operationalization: For agreed class-3 rules, flip one cell on a random background and measure the fraction of the light cone that eventually differs. Confirm uncontrolled spread if the difference reaches essentially the whole cone; the further claim that this makes component-style proofs very difficult is supported only as a record of which proof techniques succeed.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: damage-spreading experiments on class-3 rules such as rule 30

obstacles: Very difficult is a judgment about proof search, and a later successful construction would not erase the historical difficulty.
Class 3 itself is a visual category, so membership of borderline rules is not unique.
assessments.rationale: The spreading clause is an ordinary simulation: one-cell perturbations of rules such as rule 30 can be measured and either stay localized or fill the light cone. The clause about proofs is methodological. Simulation can show that the usual glider-component route lacks stable pieces, without showing that no proof of any kind exists.

assessments.operationalization: Universality means a computable encoding under which rule 30, and likewise rule 45, emulates every Turing machine. A published encoding would confirm each rule; a proof that some Turing computation is impossible in that rule would refute it. Equal-speed gliders on periodic backgrounds can be searched separately and do not decide the question.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: search for localized structures of rules 30 and 45, and replay of one-step block emulations

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: published rule-30 center column, a concrete sequence used in partial computational studies of the rule

obstacles: The natural glider proof used for rule 110 does not apply if every localized structure has the same velocity, but that does not decide universality.
A finite search cannot exhaust encodings, and non-universality of these rules is not known to be finitely checkable.
assessments.rationale: Both rules are fully specified, so universality is a sharp mathematical property, and pieces of evidence such as one-step emulation can be recomputed. No proof that either rule is universal or that either is not is available as a finished, checkable argument. Those partial experiments are exactly the ones the book says do not settle the prediction.

assessments.operationalization: Using the book's block encoding, search background blocks of increasing width until each of the 256 elementary rules is or is not realized for one step. Confirm if rules 22, 30, and 110 realize all 256 and rules 90 and 184 realize only a few; refute if a listed complex rule misses some target inside the searched widths, or a listed simple rule realizes many more.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: search engine for block backgrounds that reproduce one step of each elementary rule

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: statement of the encoding, including the width-5 scheme for rule 30

obstacles: A negative result is relative to this block scheme and to the width cutoff; some other encoding could still exist.
assessments.rationale: The experiment is finite once a width cutoff is fixed, and for rule 30 the book already names a small width that is supposed to cover every elementary target. Re-running that search is standard computation and either reproduces the reported split between simple and complex rules or finds a counterexample. One-step emulation remains a weaker property than universality, but that weaker property is the claim being scored.

assessments.operationalization: List the elementary rules whose typical behavior is not periodic or nested, and ask which of them emulate a Turing machine. The numerical claim is confirmed if the number of universal elementary rules is about 27, and refuted if a completed classification puts the number far from 27.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: proof covering rule 110 and its three elementary equivalents, four of the candidate rules

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: census of which elementary rules look complex enough to be in the candidate set of about 27

obstacles: Perhaps as many as is a hedged count, so only a classification far from 27 is a clear refutation.
Looking complex, and emulating one step of every elementary rule, does not prove universality.
assessments.rationale: The candidate pool of complex-looking elementary rules can be recounted by simulation, and four rules in the symmetry class of rule 110 are known to be universal. The other candidates do not have finished proofs, so the number that are in fact universal is not determined. Existing resources fix a short list and a lower bound, not the count in the claim.

assessments.operationalization: Take the published 2-state 5-color transition table and the sweep encoding of a rule-110 row. Confirm if each completed sweep updates the tape by exactly one rule-110 step; universality follows because rule 110 is universal. A sweep that mismatches rule 110 refutes the reduction.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: published 2-state 5-color machine and its emulation of rule 110

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: rule table and the compressed picture of the back-and-forth sweep

obstacles: The reduction shows universality relative to the rule-110 proof; an error in that proof would carry over.
assessments.rationale: The machine is a finite table, and the proposed emulation is a concrete head motion that can be compared with rule 110 for any number of sweeps. That comparison, together with the published universality of rule 110, is a complete proof. Both the table and the rule-110 proof are public.

assessments.operationalization: Enumerate all 4096 machines with 2 states and 2 colors and classify each evolution as halting, periodic, or otherwise finitely describable. Confirm if none can emulate a universal system; refute if one machine does.

candidate_datasets.name: Busy Beaver Challenge
candidate_datasets.role: public enumeration and deciders for small 2-symbol Turing machines, including the 2-state case

Behavior simple enough to decide in closed form cannot implement an arbitrary Turing computation. A full classification either produces a universal machine or a case-by-case proof that none exists, and that work fits in days to weeks.

assessments.operationalization: From a blank tape, enumerate the 2,985,984 machines with 2 states and 3 colors and sample the much larger 2-state 4-color and 4-state 2-color spaces. Using a fixed complexity test, estimate the complex fraction and count the equivalence class of complex 2-state 3-color machines. Rates near one in 50,000 and one in 200,000, and a class of 14, support the report; a count of a different order refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Busy Beaver Challenge
candidate_datasets.role: tools and archives for blank-tape censuses of small Turing machines

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: numbering scheme in which the 14 machines and machine 596,440 are identified

obstacles: Complex behavior is a visual category, so two reasonable classifiers can move the estimated rates.
The one-in-50,000 and one-in-200,000 figures are sampling estimates, and the spaces are too large for a naive full run at long times.
assessments.rationale: The 2-state 3-color census is a finite computation that has a definite count once complexity is formalized, and the figure of 14 equivalent machines is a specific target. The two larger rates are explicitly approximate and depend on a sample and a classifier. Reproducing the order of magnitude is feasible; pinning the exact quoted rates is not, because the predicate is not fully formal.

assessments.operationalization: Check a reduction from cyclic tag systems or Turing machines to machine 596,440, including the initial-condition encoding. Universality is confirmed if every computation is emulated and the encoding itself is not doing the computation. Simplest is confirmed only relative to a stated size measure and a completed proof that every smaller machine is non-universal.

candidate_datasets.name: Smith 2007 proof commentary
candidate_datasets.role: public outline of the proof that machine 596,440 emulates cyclic tag systems

candidate_datasets.name: Smith, Universality of Wolfram's 2, 3 Turing Machine
candidate_datasets.role: published version of the universality argument for this machine

candidate_datasets.name: Busy Beaver Challenge
candidate_datasets.role: classification of smaller 2-symbol machines against which simplest can be compared

obstacles: The proof uses a non-periodic infinite initial condition, so it can be rejected by a definition of universality that requires a periodic background.
By most measures is undefined, and 3-state 2-color machines have the same number of transitions and are not fully classified.

Whether the machine is the simplest depends on the size measure and on open neighbors such as 3-state 2-color machines, which a 2-state 2-color classification does not close. The claim as a conjunction is therefore only partly decided.

assessments.operationalization: Run all 2,985,984 machines with 3 states and 2 colors from a blank tape and classify each as quickly periodic or nested. candidate_datasets.name: Busy Beaver Challenge
candidate_datasets.role: blank-tape enumeration and deciders for 2-symbol Turing machines with few states

obstacles: Quickly and simple need time and classifier cutoffs before the blank-tape census is unique.
There are infinitely many non-blank tapes, so examples that eventually simplify do not prove the universal claim.
assessments.rationale: The blank-tape half is a finite enumeration inside the reach of existing Turing-machine deciders, and it can be redone. The claim also says that more complicated inputs still resolve into a simple form, which a blank-tape census does not address. Samples of other inputs can support or weaken that half without covering it.

assessments.operationalization: Iterate the S and K rules from the published length-8 expression and measure expression size, and separately apply the published combinator that is supposed to implement one step of rule 110. Exponential growth confirms that instance; a step-by-step match confirms the emulation. Statistical tests of the internal structure address seemingly random without proving the absence of regularity.

candidate_datasets.name: A New Kind of Science online
candidate_datasets.role: the length-8 combinator and the combinator expression stated to reproduce rule 110

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: rule-110 evolution against which the combinator reduction is compared

obstacles: Seemingly random internal structure can fail statistical tests and still have an undetected regularity.
Historical universality of combinators uses the standard S and K calculus; the pictures alone do not re-prove that theorem.
assessments.rationale: The growth of a particular short combinator and the rule-110 emulator are finite symbolic computations that can be rerun exactly. Universality of the S-K calculus is a classical theorem, and the rule-110 expression is a concrete witness linking that theorem to the pictures. The impression of randomness is the only part that statistical tests cannot finish.

assessments.operationalization: The claim says every rule-governed process may be regarded as a computation. Any process already given by definite rules satisfies that redescription, and no measurement distinguishes it from the same process described as law-governed evolution.
obstacles: Can be viewed as introduces a uniform language rather than a distinct empirical commitment.
assessments.rationale: Calling a rule-following process a computation does not add a variable, a dataset, or a forbidden outcome. Whether nature in fact follows definite rules is a different and stronger statement than the one made here. As stated, the sentence is a framework for comparison, not a claim those comparisons can test.

assessments.operationalization: Operationalize obviously simple as proved repetitive or nested behavior, and equivalent sophistication as Turing universality. Inside a finite rule family, estimate the fraction of non-simple rules that are universal. The principle is supported if that fraction is near one across families and if sampled natural processes match it, and it is refuted by a large class of non-simple, non-universal processes.

candidate_datasets.name: UniversalityDB
candidate_datasets.role: partial census of systems proved universal, the proposed single highest level

candidate_datasets.name: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Church-Turing thesis
candidate_datasets.role: background distinction between one maximal computable level and intermediate degrees

obstacles: Almost all, obviously simple, and sophistication admit several formalizations, including intermediate degrees and complexity classes.
A system can look complex for decades without a universality proof, and that delay is compatible with the principle.
assessments.rationale: Restricted to a small formal family, the principle becomes a statement about what fraction of non-simple rules are universal, and a few rules on each side are already classified. assessments.rationale: The sentence is a conditional theorem, and the proof is the standard one: completeness plus consistency is itself a decision procedure for the string-or-negation question. assessments.operationalization: For each named system, use a published proof or decision procedure: propositional logic and pure monadic predicate logic are decidable, arithmetic and set theory interpret computation, the word problem for groups is undecidable, and Tarski's real algebra and elementary geometry are decidable. The clause about every system used in research is scored only relative to an explicit list of fields.

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formalized developments of logic, arithmetic, and set theory used to check which standard systems interpret computation

candidate_datasets.name: TPTP
candidate_datasets.role: public collection of axiom systems across mathematical domains, a partial census of systems in actual formal use

obstacles: Used in current research is a sociological boundary rather than a formal list.
Universality is proved theory by theory, so the universal quantifier needs a census.
The exceptions for commutative groups, real algebra, and geometry have to be applied uniformly.
assessments.rationale: The named positive and negative cases are classical theorems, and proof libraries contain formalizations of several of them. The sentence also says that every axiom system in actual research use, outside a list of heavily constrained exceptions, is universal. There is no canonical public census of that class, so the theorems settle the examples and leave the quantifier partly checked.

assessments.operationalization: Enumerate equational axioms up to a length cutoff, reject those with finite models incompatible with a candidate universal algebra, and attempt universality proofs for the survivors. A high density of proved non-universal systems above the cutoff would challenge the claim; a high density of unproved candidates would leave it open.

candidate_datasets.name: Mace4
candidate_datasets.role: finite-model finder for screening short equational axioms for multiple non-isomorphic models

candidate_datasets.name: TPTP
candidate_datasets.role: library of equational and first-order problems against which small candidate axiom systems can be compared

obstacles: Finite-model screening can refute a candidate and cannot prove universality.
Almost any and a low threshold are not a specified density.
A decidable theory above a proposed cutoff is a local exception the word almost can absorb.
assessments.rationale: Finite-model finders can survey the shortest axiom systems and show that many are not pinned to a single operator, which counts against universality for those systems. Proving universality is a separate obligation, and it is sparse. The expectation that almost any axiom system past a low threshold is universal remains a conjecture, with the survey covering only the bottom of the ordering.

assessments.operationalization: Verify that solutions of the stated exponential Diophantine equation encode rule 110 histories, using the published proof that rule 110 is universal, and apply the standard translation from an undecidable cellular-automaton question to a statement independent of arithmetic. A break in the encoding refutes this derivation; a checked encoding confirms it.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: proof that rule 110 is universal, the step from which undecidable arithmetic statements are derived

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formalized incompleteness of arithmetic, the conclusion this encoding is supposed to reach

obstacles: The displayed exponential Diophantine equation is large, so checking every clause is specialist work.
Other proofs of incompleteness exist, so a gap in this encoding would refute the route rather than incompleteness itself.
assessments.rationale: Both ingredients are published and checkable: rule 110 is universal by Cook's proof, and incompleteness of arithmetic is a formalized theorem. The distinctive step is the integer equation that emulates rule 110, which is explicit and is a finite certificate a proof-oriented check can accept or reject. The claim is this implication, and the resources to check it exist.

assessments.operationalization: Fix a size measure such as number of variables and total degree, then search for an equation below a stated size whose insolubility is provable in a standard metatheory and unprovable in ordinary arithmetic. Exhibiting one confirms the existence claim at that size; a proof that every equation below the size is decidable in arithmetic would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formal arithmetic in which an explicit independence proof for a Diophantine statement would be checked

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: published smallest solutions of simple Diophantine equations, a size baseline against known universal equations

obstacles: Rather simple needs an explicit size cutoff.
Known universal equations are large, and proving a specific small equation independent of arithmetic is a separate theorem.
A true Pi-1 statement can be independent, so failure to find a solution below a search bound is inconclusive.
assessments.rationale: The existence of some Diophantine equations with unprovable insolubility follows from the DPRM theorem plus incompleteness, and the known universal examples are the complicated ones the text describes. The further claim that rather simple equations of this kind exist is an existence conjecture with no supplied witness. Catalogs of small equations support the contrast in size and do not exhibit an independent simple case.

assessments.operationalization: Fix a list of unsolved problems studied in number theory and determine what fraction are independent of the usual axioms of arithmetic. Each problem is independent or it is not; producing those independence results is a family of proofs, and computation of special cases does not yield them.
obstacles: Independence of a specific arithmetic statement is not produced by computation or by the absence of a known proof.
A fair fraction and seriously studied require a closed list the claim does not give.
A proof in a stronger theory leaves open whether arithmetic alone sufficed.
assessments.rationale: Once a list is fixed, each problem is independent of arithmetic or it is not, so the sentence is not empty. Public mathematics contains independence proofs for carefully built statements, and it does not decide the open problems number theorists study. Computation and observation do not generate those independence proofs, so the predicted fraction cannot be resolved with resources that exist now.

assessments.operationalization: Assemble a list of mathematical areas and, in each, separate questions with decision procedures from questions reduced to the halting problem. The pattern supports the claim where undecidability begins immediately past the decidable fragment, and challenges it where a large intermediate band stays decidable.

candidate_datasets.name: TPTP
candidate_datasets.role: cross-domain library of axiomatized problems, a sample of where decision procedures do and do not exist

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formalized map of which standard theories interpret arithmetic and therefore inherit undecidability

obstacles: Always easy and practically any area are not formal thresholds.
Known undecidability results concentrate in fields logicians chose to encode computation into.
A decidable theory with difficult questions counts as a counterexample only after easy is defined.
assessments.rationale: Surveys and problem libraries document undecidability in group theory, tilings, Diophantine equations, topology, and other fields, and they also document large decidable theories. That literature can test the pattern inside studied areas. It does not measure almost as soon as questions stop being easy across practically any area, because both the threshold and the inventory of areas are unspecified.

assessments.operationalization: Compare questions mathematicians emphasize with a neutral sample of questions about simple formal systems, and test whether the emphasized set is the decidable subset. The claim provides neither the sample nor a measure of emphasis.
obstacles: Defined itself to avoid encodes an intention that publication records omit.
An uncharacteristic sample needs a measure on all possible mathematics.
The same publication record fits difficulty, taste, and applicability as causes.
assessments.rationale: The sentence is a historical thesis: mathematics selected questions its proof methods can answer, so the present subject is a small uncharacteristic sample of what is possible. Classification databases record what was studied. They do not record why alternatives were set aside, and they do not encode the space of possible systems, so rival histories fit the same record.

assessments.operationalization: Fix a length-preserving involution as negation and prove or refute that a multiway system is complete and consistent exactly when it eventually generates half the strings of each length from the string for true. A counterexample involution, or a gap in the pairing argument, refutes the biconditional; a checked proof confirms it.

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formal logic library in which the pairing argument about negation, consistency, and completeness can be machine-checked

obstacles: An involution with fixed points breaks the identification of exactly half with completeness plus consistency.
For a concrete rule, the eventual fraction of strings may itself be undecidable; the general implication is what the proof settles.
assessments.rationale: Under a fixed-point-free length-preserving negation, strings come in pairs, so generating more than half forces a string and its negation, and generating less than half leaves some pair untouched. That is a short combinatorial argument and can be formalized with standard tools. The criterion for this class of multiway systems is therefore settleable by proof now; computing the fraction for one irreducible rule is a different and often undecidable question.

assessments.operationalization: For a standard system, estimate the density of sentences the axioms decide under a stated length measure, and inspect how explicitly other models can be described. A large, easily described set of independent sentences would challenge close to complete; a density near one half on each side of negation would support it for that system.

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formalized body of theorems in arithmetic and set theory, a lower bound on what standard axioms actually decide

candidate_datasets.name: TPTP
candidate_datasets.role: axiomizations of algebraic theories, including groups, whose bare axioms decide much less than a theory of one specific structure

obstacles: Fair fraction and close to complete need a measure on statements.
Nonstandard models of arithmetic are known to exist and are also non-constructive, so obscure stays a judgment.
The raw group axioms are highly incomplete until further axioms pick out a specific group.
assessments.rationale: Model theory and formal libraries give real information: arithmetic decides ordinary number-theoretic statements and its other models are not explicit, while some textbook systems, such as the bare group axioms, decide much less. Fair fraction and usually are not tied to a measure or a closed list of systems. These results test examples rather than the general claim.

assessments.operationalization: Enumerate short equational axioms for one binary operator and, with a finite-model finder, list the multiplication tables on two, three, and four elements that satisfy each axiom. The claim holds if, under an explicit simplicity ordering, most axioms admit many inequivalent tables and only a few force a single table.

candidate_datasets.name: Mace4
candidate_datasets.role: finite-model finder that enumerates the operator tables satisfying a short equational axiom

obstacles: Vast majority depends on the length cutoff and the ordering of axioms.
Isomorphism pruning on three and four elements changes counts and leaves a qualitative majority meaningful.
Finite domains omit operators whose only distinguishing models are infinite.
assessments.rationale: The observation is a finite model-enumeration of the kind Mace4 performs, matching the book's tables for two, three, and four elements. A re-run either reproduces a strong majority of multi-model axioms or it does not. Infinite models are a further question; the claim as illustrated is about these finite operator forms, and that enumeration is feasible now.

assessments.operationalization: Search single equations with at most six Nands, test which small finite operators they allow, and confirm a survivor by a proof that it axiomatizes propositional logic. Finding such an axiom among the shortest few thousand candidates, and none shorter, supports the claim; a gap in the equivalence proof removes that candidate.

candidate_datasets.name: Mace4
candidate_datasets.role: finite-model screening of short single axioms to see which allow only Nand and Nor on small domains

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: formal propositional logic in which equivalence of a short Nand axiom to the standard calculus can be checked

obstacles: The simplest few thousand depends on the enumeration order of axioms.
Allowing only Nand and Nor on a small domain is a screen; equivalence to propositional logic still needs a proof.
assessments.rationale: Short single axioms for Nand logic are a finite search plus a proof of equivalence, both standard, and both carried through for the six-Nand axioms. Model finders reproduce the screening step, and a formal derivation can check that a candidate axiomatizes propositional logic. The likelihood remark is then the position of those axioms in the same enumeration.

assessments.operationalization: Pick a formal property meant to mark the traditional axiom systems and ask whether simple unused systems share it and support a comparable body of results. The claim states no such property and no measure of richness.
obstacles: Fundamentally special and as rich are evaluative.
Any formal property traditional systems share can be copied by another formal system, which leaves the practical claim untouched.
assessments.rationale: The conclusion is that history, rather than a formal distinction, selected the axiom systems of existing mathematics, and that other systems could found equally rich fields. Richness and specialness are judgments about a practice. Sharing a formal property with a simple multiway system does not decide whether that system founds a field, so the sentence has no discriminating measurement.

assessments.operationalization: Generate propositional tautologies in order of increasing expression size and mark those not entailed by the conjunction of earlier ones. Compare that set with the named Boolean laws in a fixed collection of logic textbooks. A close match confirms the claim; a large symmetric difference refutes it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Logic Project
candidate_datasets.role: open textbook corpus of named laws of propositional logic to compare with the non-derivability filter

obstacles: A different corpus of textbooks could name a different subset.
The second distributive law is derivable from earlier theorems and is still traditionally named, so almost exactly needs a stated tolerance.
assessments.rationale: Propositional entailment is decidable, so the filter that keeps theorems not implied by simpler ones is an ordinary computation, and the named laws are a small explicit list. Open textbooks supply those names. Corpus choice is a limited confound and can be fixed in advance, so the comparison can be run now and can confirm or refute the reported match.

assessments.operationalization: Build the dependence graph of a formal library, measure reuse and path-shortening, and compare those measures with independent ratings of depth or power and with a contrast between a compact algebraic field and elementary number theory. Agreement would support the suspicion; a reversed pattern would challenge it.

candidate_datasets.name: Lean mathlib
candidate_datasets.role: large public dependency graph of formalized theorems across several fields

candidate_datasets.name: Metamath Proof Explorer
candidate_datasets.role: second formal library whose theorem network can be compared with mathlib

obstacles: There is no public dataset of mathematicians' ratings for difficult, powerful, surprising, or deep.
Formal libraries over-represent fields chosen for formalization, which favors compact networks.
A successful area is partly identified by the same judgments the network is asked to explain.
assessments.rationale: Proof libraries are public graphs of statements and dependencies, so network compactness can be measured for mathematics that has been formalized. They do not contain a controlled set of intuitive labels, and they are a biased sample of fields that formalize well. The comparison with elementary number theory is a partial proxy for the suspicion about sparser networks.

assessments.operationalization: For each candidate feature, such as learning, adaptation, or abstraction, either exhibit it in a system nobody counts as intelligent or show that humans lack it. Any finite list of features leaves open whether some other general definition works.
obstacles: A proposed definition can be revised after each counterexample.
Workable, and what we normally think of as intelligence, are judgments.
assessments.rationale: Memory-like persistence in a cellular automaton or a fluid is easy to simulate and puts pressure on particular proposed marks of intelligence. The sentence concludes that every workable definition must collapse into human particulars. Failed proposals do not distinguish that conclusion from the existence of a definition not yet stated.

assessments.operationalization: Take a stated feature, such as self-reproduction, self-organization, or high morphological complexity, and search small cellular automata for a rule that meets a formal criterion for it. Success supports the occurrence claim for that feature; the conclusion about how observers recognize life is a further question.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: simulator for additive rules such as rule 90 and outer-totalistic code 204, which reproduce patterns, and for other simple self-organizing rules

obstacles: A feature can be redefined so that the simple system fails it.
Recognized as life is a human judgment.
Self-reproduction in an additive rule is a thin case of the biological notion.
assessments.rationale: Additive rules such as elementary rule 90 and the two-dimensional totalistic rule in the text visibly copy patterns, and simulators make that check routine. Similar exhibitions exist for pattern formation. The step from these examples to almost any proposed feature of life, and to the conclusion that only Earth-like chemical detail counts, is not a result those simulations close.

assessments.operationalization: Compare compressibility or geometric regularity of human-designed objects with natural objects in matched shape or image corpora. A robust simplicity gap is the surface prediction. The causal clause, that engineers must foresee behavior, needs a contrast with designed objects that were not required to be predictable.

candidate_datasets.name: ShapeNet
candidate_datasets.role: public 3D models of human-designed objects, a corpus for measuring geometric simplicity of artifacts

candidate_datasets.name: iNaturalist
candidate_datasets.role: public photographs of organisms, a partial corpus of natural forms for comparison with designed objects

obstacles: Artifact and organism collections are unmatched samples.
Materials, style, and function produce simple forms without any appeal to computational reducibility.
A photograph does not measure whether a natural system is computationally irreducible.
assessments.rationale: Public shape and organism repositories can support a statistical comparison of how regular designed objects look relative to natural ones, which is the observable surface of the claim. They do not record whether a designer needed a predictive theory, and many non-computational constraints produce simple artifacts. The available comparison is a proxy with serious confounds.

assessments.operationalization: Given a feature, test whether the observed rule is minimal among rules that produce it, and treat minimality as evidence of purpose. The text notes that an unguided exhaustive search can find the same minimum, so the observation fits design and blind search alike.
obstacles: The claim says purpose can be redescribed as mechanism, so behavior never identifies purpose with certainty.
Seem more likely is a degree of suspicion rather than a decision threshold.
A minimal rule can be the output of a purposeless search.
assessments.rationale: Minimality is a computable property once a feature is formalized. The sentence uses it as a sign of purpose, while also saying that purposes can be rewritten as mechanisms and that a purposeless search can discover minimal rules. Those concessions leave no outcome that favors creation-for-a-purpose over a rival that denies purpose.

assessments.operationalization: On signals independently known to be communications of a non-human technological civilization, measure repetition, spectral lines, and compressibility. Essentially no detectable regularities would support the claim for ongoing traffic; stable recognizable carriers in that traffic would refute it. Beacons meant to be noticed are excluded and scored separately.

candidate_datasets.name: Breakthrough Listen
candidate_datasets.role: public radio search for narrowband technosignatures, which archives emission and non-detections rather than confirmed extraterrestrial messages

candidate_datasets.name: Berkeley SETI Research Center
candidate_datasets.role: public description and data access for radio SETI surveys, including Breakthrough Listen

obstacles: A noise-like spectrum is the prediction both for compressed messages and for ordinary astrophysical emission.
No confirmed extraterrestrial communication corpus exists.
The beacon exception makes non-detection of carriers compatible with the claim.
assessments.rationale: Radio surveys publicly archive astronomical emission and the results of narrowband searches. They do not contain messages identified as extraterrestrial communications, which is the variable the prediction concerns. Until such a corpus exists, a noise-like recording fits both the claim and the hypothesis that the recording is natural.

assessments.operationalization: Fix a measure of computation and compare a model of turbulence in stellar gas with an estimate for recorded human calculation, and separately exhibit non-designed systems that output the primes. The primes half is immediate; the turbulence comparison is only approximated by existing flow databases.

candidate_datasets.name: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases
candidate_datasets.role: public direct numerical simulations of turbulent flows, a proxy for how much computation a turbulent fluid performs

candidate_datasets.name: OEIS
candidate_datasets.role: published prime sequence, generated by short non-intelligent procedures

obstacles: Amount of computation is left as most measures, and those measures disagree.
Laboratory turbulence is a proxy for gas around a star, and human intellectual history is not a standard dataset.
A short prime generator settles only the easier half of the claim.
assessments.rationale: A short program, and the recorded prime sequence, show that primes are produced by systems with no claim to intelligence, so that half is resolvable by computation. The stellar-turbulence comparison is quantitative and physical. Public turbulence databases support order-of-magnitude estimates for earthly flows, and they do not settle an accounting of computation around a star against human intellectual history.

assessments.operationalization: The sentence says the task is to find systems whose details are close enough to humans that we call them intelligent. A system we do not recognize is then either not intelligent or not similar, and the claim does not separate those readings.
obstacles: Recognition of intelligence is defined by similarity to humans, so a dissimilar intelligence falls outside the criterion.
Likely to exist is not tied to an observation.
assessments.rationale: This is a conclusion about what would count as recognizing intelligence, rather than a forecast with a separate measurement. Generalized intelligence that behaves in unhuman ways is, by the sentence's own standard, something we would not count as intelligence. No astronomical or biological dataset distinguishes that stance from rivals.

assessments.operationalization: Count classes of systems used in engineered artifacts against an explicit enumeration of simple programs, scoring how predictable each class is. That estimates the historical fraction. The prediction that complex simple-rule behavior will make a vast amount of new technology possible is scored only when that technology exists.

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: enumeration of small programs whose range of behavior can be compared with the repetitive mechanisms used in traditional design

obstacles: The space of possible systems has no canonical measure, so a tiny fraction moves with the measure.
Vast new technology is a future outcome and is absent from present datasets.
Unrepresentative can mean unlike nature or unlike simple programs, and those comparisons differ.
assessments.rationale: Enumerations of small programs show a large range of behavior outside the repetitive mechanisms traditional design prefers, which partly checks tiny and unrepresentative. The industrially relevant measure of possible systems is not fixed. The forward claim about a vast amount of new technology is a prediction without a present outcome to score.

assessments.operationalization: Assemble, by a simple chemical process, a lattice whose update is rule 110 or an equivalent universal cellular automaton, with one or a few atoms or molecules per cell, and run a non-trivial computation. Success would confirm the claim. Existing DNA-tile automata confirm a coarser molecular construction.

candidate_datasets.name: Rothemund, Papadakis, and Winfree 2004, Algorithmic self-assembly of DNA Sierpinski triangles
candidate_datasets.role: experimental demonstration that DNA tiles can self-assemble a cellular-automaton pattern, a weaker relative of an atomic rule 110 computer

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: reference simulator for the rule 110 behavior a molecular device would need to match

obstacles: DNA tiles show programmed self-assembly of a nested pattern, not a universal computer with one atom per cell.
Plausible and likely have no numerical threshold.
A failed laboratory attempt is compatible with the claim that some simple chemical process could succeed.
assessments.rationale: DNA self-assembly has produced cellular-automaton-like patterns, including Sierpinski triangles, so a chemical medium that carries simple-rule computation is already experimental fact at molecular scale. The sentence specifies a rule 110-like universal computer at one or a few atoms per cell, assembled by a simple chemical process. That object is not in any public dataset, and the coarser demonstrations constrain plausibility only weakly.

assessments.operationalization: On a fixed suite of simple-program targets, compare exhaustive enumeration with constraint solving, heuristic search, and directed mutation, scoring how often each returns a correct short program. A non-exhaustive method that reliably matches the exhaustive search refutes the only-reliable-way reading on that suite.

candidate_datasets.name: Mace4
candidate_datasets.role: constraint-style search for finite algebras, a non-exhaustive method for some inverse problems about rules

candidate_datasets.name: Golly
candidate_datasets.role: enumerator of small cellular automata, the exhaustive baseline for the same targets

obstacles: Reliable and desired behavior need a benchmark the claim does not state.
Success of a constraint encoding on some targets leaves other targets untouched.
Worst-case irreducibility can force a search even when typical cases are easy.
assessments.rationale: Program-synthesis and finite-model tools already find some short rules without listing every rule, so the absolute wording can be probed on concrete targets with public software. Computational irreducibility still implies that some targets have no route shorter than a search. A benchmark represents only its suite, so the result tests part of a universal methodological claim.

assessments.operationalization: Take universality as the level of sophistication: a system matches the ceiling of effective procedure if it emulates a universal computer under a stated encoding. Rule 110 meets this by proof. The same standard applied to a brain model, a turbulent flow, and a candidate law of physics is not settled by existing data.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: proof that a simple cellular automaton reaches the universality ceiling used as the measure of sophistication

candidate_datasets.name: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Databases
candidate_datasets.role: resolved turbulent flows whose complexity can be inspected and whose universality is not thereby established

obstacles: Universality is proved for some cellular automata and is open for brains, turbulence, and the universe.
Similar-looking complexity is compatible with failure to emulate a universal computer.
A brain or a fluid could fail to be universal while its behavior looks complex.
assessments.rationale: For simple programs the comparison is a theorem: rule 110 is universal, so it meets the computational ceiling usually assigned to any effective procedure. Brains, turbulence, and the universe are part of the sentence and are not known to be universal on public data. Simulations of turbulence show complex flow, which leaves emulation power undecided.

assessments.operationalization: If the dynamics under study are a universal computation, no predictor that is itself an effective process computes every consequence faster than the system produces them. A universality proof discharges that conditional for systems such as rule 110. An explicit shortcut for all consequences of our universe's rules would refute the application to science, and no such pair of rules and shortcut is in hand.

candidate_datasets.name: Cook 2004, Universality in Elementary Cellular Automata
candidate_datasets.role: proof of universality used in the conditional argument that a universal system cannot be systematically outrun

obstacles: A claim that science never predicts everything has no finite observational cutoff.
The outrunning argument applies to universal systems, and whether the universe is one is open.
Success on reducible questions is compatible with a permanent limit and with the absence of one.
assessments.rationale: The conditional limit is the emulation argument already available for universal cellular automata: a system that can emulate its predictor cannot be systematically outrun. The sentence applies that limit to science as such, which requires the systems science studies, or the universe, to be irreducible in this strong sense. Nothing now public establishes that physical hypothesis, and a run of successful predictions leaves a claim about everything undecided.
